title: The Strait of Hormuz: How 34 km of Water Holds the World Hostage
description:
A strip of water between Iran and Oman, about 34 kilometres wide at its narrowest, carried about 20 million barrels of oil a day before the war. Since the US and Israel began striking Iran on 28 February 2026, it has been closed, half-open, mined, cleared and attacked again. Here is the geography, what flows through it, what happened this year, why it matters so much to India, and what to watch next.

Facts as reported up to 1 November 2026, from the IEA, the US EIA, Reuters, Al Jazeera, gCaptain and others (sources below). The war is ongoing and details may change.

Maps: country borders as shown by the Survey of India (Natural Earth, India view). Satellite imagery: NASA Blue Marble; contains modified Copernicus Sentinel data 2025-2026.
core_message: A 34 km strait carries a fifth of the world's oil, and the 2026 war has shown how little room there is around it.
comment_question: Should India build more ways around Hormuz, or more oil reserves at home?

scenes.narration: Before this year, about twenty million barrels of oil passed every single day through one narrow gap between Iran and Oman.
scenes.heading: The Strait of Hormuz

scenes.narration: Since the end of February 2026, that gap has been a war zone.
scenes.broll_query: oil tanker at sea Persian Gulf

scenes.narration: Tankers have been hit by drones, mines, missiles and speedboats. Seafarers have been killed. In March, oil prices rose faster than in any month on record.
scenes.text: The biggest monthly oil price jump on record

scenes.narration: So how does a strip of water this narrow hold the world economy hostage? And why does it matter so much to India?
Here it is from space. The Persian Gulf is almost a closed sea. Its only way out to the open ocean is this one bend: the Strait of Hormuz.
scenes.heading: The Gulf's only way out

scenes.narration: At its narrowest, between Iran's coast and Oman's Musandam peninsula, it is only about thirty-four kilometres across.
scenes.heading: About 34 km across

scenes.narration: And big ships can't use all of that. They follow two lanes, one in and one out, each only about three kilometres wide, with a buffer of water between them.
scenes.text: Two lanes, each about 3 km wide

scenes.narration: Those lanes bend right past Iran's islands, Qeshm and Larak, and its biggest naval port, Bandar Abbas.
scenes.heading: Iran's side of the strait

scenes.narration: From these islands and this coast, every passing ship is within easy reach.
In 2025, about twenty million barrels of crude oil and fuel went through here every day, according to the International Energy Agency.
scenes.heading: Through Hormuz every day in 2025

scenes.narration: That is about a quarter of all the oil the world trades by sea.
scenes.heading: Share of the world's seaborne oil trade

scenes.narration: It comes from Saudi Arabia, Iraq, Kuwait, the United Arab Emirates, Qatar, Bahrain and Iran itself. Kuwait, Qatar and Bahrain have no other way to the open sea at all.
scenes.heading: Who ships through Hormuz

scenes.narration: It isn't just oil. About a fifth of the world's liquefied natural gas goes the same way, most of it from Qatar.
scenes.text: About 1 in 5 cargoes of the world's LNG

scenes.narration: A gas tanker leaving Qatar's Ras Laffan terminal has to sail down the Gulf and out through the strait before it can reach a single customer.
scenes.heading: Out of the Gulf

scenes.narration: And most of it heads east. About eighty percent of the oil goes to Asia. China and India together took forty-four percent.
scenes.text: 80% to Asia, 44% to China and India

scenes.narration: For India, Hormuz is the front door. From the strait, a tanker can reach the giant refineries at Jamnagar in Gujarat in a few days.
scenes.heading: India's front door

scenes.narration: On the twenty-eighth of February 2026, the United States and Israel began strikes on Iran. Iran's Supreme Leader, Ali Khamenei, was killed.
Iran fired back with missiles, and its Revolutionary Guards radioed ships in the strait that none would be allowed through.
Traffic collapsed within days. By early March, insurers had withdrawn cover, so even ships willing to take the risk could not sail.
Brent crude passed one hundred dollars a barrel on the eighth of March, for the first time in four years, and peaked at about one hundred and twenty-six.
scenes.heading: Brent crude at its 2026 peak

scenes.narration: By April, the International Maritime Organization counted about two thousand ships and twenty thousand seafarers stuck inside the Gulf.
Countries opened their emergency reserves. On the eleventh of March, members of the International Energy Agency agreed to release four hundred million barrels.
What followed was a cycle. A ceasefire in April. Failed talks, and an American blockade of Iran's own ports. A deal to end the war in June. And in July, collapse.
scenes.heading: Deals that didn't hold

scenes.narration: Iran says it decides who passes. In May it set up its own authority to regulate the strait, and it has said it wants ships to pay for passage.
scenes.heading: Iran's claim to the strait

scenes.narration: Ships from some countries, including China, India and Pakistan, have been let through. Ships trading with the United States, Israel and their allies were told to stay out.
Under the water there was another danger. More than a hundred suspected mines were found in the shipping lanes, and American officials said in late August that the lanes had been cleared.
scenes.heading: Mines in the lanes

scenes.narration: Ships started moving again. By the end of September, the Middle East was exporting about eighteen million barrels of crude a day, about what it shipped before the war, according to the analytics firm Kpler.
scenes.text: Exports back to about 18M barrels a day

scenes.narration: But the attacks didn't stop. October brought near-daily strikes on ships in and around the strait.
On the sixth of October, the tanker On Peace was hit about nine nautical miles off Limah, on Oman's coast, and caught fire.
scenes.heading: On Peace, 6 October

scenes.narration: Nineteen crew were on board, seventeen of them Indian. At least twelve were injured. Nobody claimed the attack.
India says at least ten Indian seafarers have been killed since the war began.

On the fourteenth of October, a Singapore-flagged container ship, the GFS Pride, sank near the strait. Security sources said a projectile hit it; Iran's Revolutionary Guards blamed a mine. At the end of the month, a speedboat attack set a tanker's engine room on fire.
scenes.text: A container ship sunk, a tanker set ablaze

scenes.narration: Even with oil flowing, Brent crude was at about a hundred and one dollars in early October. The day before the war began, it was seventy-two.
scenes.heading: Brent crude, dollars a barrel

scenes.narration: Is there a way around? Partly. Saudi Arabia can pump crude across the desert to Yanbu on the Red Sea, through a pipeline built for five million barrels a day.
scenes.heading: Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline

scenes.narration: The UAE has its own pipeline to Fujairah, on the far side of the strait, which can carry about one point eight million.
scenes.heading: The UAE's pipeline to Fujairah

scenes.narration: But together, they can only take part of the twenty million barrels a day that used to sail through. The IEA puts the room left in them at three and a half to five and a half million.
Qatar's gas has no pipeline around the strait at all. And Bangladesh, India and Pakistan got almost two thirds of their imported LNG through the strait last year.
At the end of October, Qatari mediators gave Iran a new draft deal to end the war: a seven-day schedule of steps, with other countries as guarantors. Iran was considering it.
So three things will decide what happens next. Whether a deal holds. Whether the attacks on ships stop. And whether insurers are willing to cover ships again.
scenes.heading: What to watch
items: Do the attacks on ships stop?

scenes.narration: Thirty-four kilometres of water. Still the most important shortcut on Earth, and right now, the most fragile.
scenes.heading: The world's most fragile shortcut

scenes.narration: Should India build more ways around Hormuz, or keep more oil in reserve at home? Tell us in the comments.
